episodes.211263: Showers and weak thunderstorms generated high winds across portions of central and north central South Dakota from the afternoon of April 22nd into the early morning hours of April 23rd. A peak wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at the Sand Lake RAWS 13 miles east northeast of Eureka, and at the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 5 miles north of Reliance. Winds were strong enough 5 miles east of Pollock to flatten a 10 by 10 outbuilding and gazebo, and power poles were snapped 6 miles north northeast of Eureka, with a loss of power to 615 customers. Power outages were also reported in Walworth county to 108 customers. The lightning overnight sparked a 30 acre fire near the town of Barnard in Brown county.
episodes.211348: Severe t-storms developed during the late afternoon into the evening of April 23rd.  Large hail, damaging winds and a few tornadoes were documented.  The strongest tornado damaged structures at lake kahola near the Morris and Chase County line.  The other tornadoes were rated EF0 or EFU due to lack of documented damage.
episodes.211414: Ahead of a strong low pressure system, hot temperatures, just enough humid air, and an unstable atmosphere, created widespread showers and scattered thunderstorms, some of which included severe wind gusts for many locations.
episodes.211681: Isolated severe storms developed over portions of SE Texas. These storms produced extensive damage to utility lines across Jackson County.
episodes.211702: Isolated thunderstorms moved through south central North Dakota in an atmosphere with a very dry and deep sub-cloud layer. This led to random severe wind gusts with a few of the storms. The strongest reported wind gust was 72 mph which occurred near Wishek in McIntosh County.
episodes.211771: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
episodes.211789: A line of severe thunderstorms produced a 61 mph wind gust in Grant County during the evening hours on April 23rd. Additionally, some outbuilding damage was noted in Monroe County due to strong winds from these storms.
episodes.212573: A deepening low-pressure system located across the western Canadian Prairies moved into Manitoba on April 23rd, 2026. A surface cold front associated with this low was stretched across Minnesota. This aided the development of showers and thunderstorms that afternoon. A few stronger storms did produce large hail measuring quarter size (Freeborn Co.) and half-dollar size (Meeker Co.). Additionally, in southern Minnesota, the AWOS station located in Albert Lea measured a 62-mph wind gust.
episodes.212659: Severe thunderstorms produced wind gusts up to 60 mph over parts of the Devils Lake Basin in northeast ND during the late evening hours on April 22.
episodes.213010: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.

episodes.213035: A line of thunderstorms developed across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 23rd. Several landspout tornadoes occurred as this line of thunderstorms moved across portions central and south-central Kansas.
episodes.213125: An advancing strong cold front sparked scattered afternoon storms. Strongest storms took advantage of 1500-2000 J/kg MLCAPE and 40 knots of effective shear to produce large hail.
episodes.213343: Severe thunderstorms developed and moved across western SD and brought strong, damaging wind gusts to the Black Hills. Storms consolidated into a line and produced strong wind gusts further east.

A tornado developed approximately 1.5 miles north-northwest of Little Sioux, IA at 12:46 PM CST. The tornado began just southeast of the intersection of 120th Street and Dayton Avenue, before flipping a center pivot. It continued northeast, damaging farm outbuildings, trees, and power poles near 120th Street and Early Avenue. Just over 1 mile northeast of this intersection, another center pivot was flipped over. The tornado then turned slightly more eastward and tore the fabric roofing off part of a hoop barn near Gage Lane and Easton Trail. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 105 mph.

Several videos and photographs from multiple angles indicated that a weak tornado developed and moved to the east northeast along this approximate path. While the near-surface dust cloud was wider, the core circulation was quite narrow and weak. The only damage along the track was minor tree damage as it crossed mostly open fields. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 70 mph.

NWS damage survey revealed a small tornado did damage to a single family home and a few outbuildings and cabins on the northeast side of Lake Kahola.  The short damage path was discontinuous with portions of the short track having been untouched.   The greatest degree of damage occurred to outbuildings that were destroyed and walls were tossed into another cabin.   This tornado was rated a EF1 with winds to around 110 mph.
The report was relayed through mPING.
